Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
frontier.abstract: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.

frontier.title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
frontier.abstract: We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent that we use for research on problems whose answers aprogram or data can check. Each candidate solution is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox; proposers see only a public score, and a private split decides what counts. The harness itself(prompts, tools, skills, playbook, meta agent) is an editable genome, changed only through a kernel-enforced gate with held-out and cost checks. An autonomous mode goes from a plain-text goal to a verified report with no human step: an agent picks an open problem and writes its verifier, the kernel calibrates it, an adversarial agent audits it, and an agent that never sees the verifier re-checks the result. Across fourteen problems in six days, for about $180 of model usage, the system produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information: a certified depolarizing-channel threshold point p = 0.064966, a qutrit positivity frontier of 0.2910672, a 44-gate depth-6 Golay state preparation, and a stabilizer-rank bound chi(T^7) <= 10. It also cut SABRE qubit-routing overhead from 68,559 to 12,087 added gates. In hardware, it cut the energy per MAC of an open 8x8 INT8 systolic tile by 77.7% through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow, bit-exact. Three fully autonomous runs ended in honestties with public records; one audit caught a stale record, and one agent-written score pointing the wrong way went unnoticed. We report the failures as carefully: the one self-derived harness generation was rejected on cost, proposers gamed lenient scorers four times, and operator changes were decisive for several results.

frontier.title: WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU
frontier.abstract: Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model's positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk's memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.

frontier.title: GenTranslate: Large Language Models are Generative Multilingual Speech and Machine Translators
frontier.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have stepped forward the development of multilingual speech and machine translation by its reduced representation errors and incorporated external knowledge. However, both translation tasks typically utilize beam search decoding and top-1 hypothesis selection for inference. These techniques struggle to fully exploit the rich information in the diverse N-best hypotheses, making them less optimal for translation tasks that require a single, high-quality output sequence. In this paper, we propose a new generative paradigm for translation tasks, namely GenTranslate, which builds upon LLMs to generate better results from the diverse translation versions in N-best list. Leveraging the rich linguistic knowledge and strong reasoning abilities of LLMs, our new paradigm can integrate the diverse N-best candidates to generate a higher-quality translation result. Furthermore, to support LLM finetuning, we build and release a HypoTranslate dataset that contains over 592K hypotheses-translation pairs in 11 languages. Experiments on various speech and machine translation benchmarks (e.g., FLEURS, CoVoST-2, WMT) demonstrate that our GenTranslate significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art model.

frontier.title: Agent-as-a-Verifier: From Scores to Evidence for General Verification
frontier.abstract: Verification is increasingly critical across various inference and learning paradigms, such as test-time scaling, recursive intelligence and automated research, where feedback can improve efficiency and optimization. Common score-based verifiers, or discriminative reward models, predict a scalar reward for an output. While useful for filtering, rewarding, and ranking, such scores provide no explicit, auditable evidentiary basis for the judgment. In parallel, although existing generative process reward models offer text feedback, most designs do not fully exploit agentic capabilities, such as tool use and iterative reasoning, which are essential for fact-checking and fine-grained claim verification. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing Agent-as-a-Verifier, an agentic, certificate-producing verification system that places role-separated LLM agents inside a formal-methods-inspired claim-obligation-certificate protocol. Given a generation candidate, Agent-as-a-Verifier produces a certificate by extracting a verdict-blind dependency graph of claims, independently compiling the task's acceptance contract, and deriving checkable obligations. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Agent-as-a-Verifier achieves higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art approach. Across different downstream applications, the augmented agent also outperforms the plain agent on FrontierMath and CyberGym. More importantly, Agent-as-a-Verifier is able to identify reward-hacking solutions that deceive the benchmark evaluator, highlighting its broader potential for iterative and recursive agent optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/sunyxedu/General-Verifier

frontier.title: AI Buckingham: Agentic Discovery of Dimensionless Scaling Laws Across Physical Regimes
frontier.abstract: Classical dimensional analysis defines admissible dimensionless representations but does not determine which combinations capture the dominant physical dependence, whether it changes across physical regimes, or when dependent-variable rescaling is required. We present AI Buckingham, an agentic framework for autonomous dimensionless discovery from natural-language descriptions of physical problems and observational data. It couples reasoning and planning by a large language model (LLM) with predefined symbolic and numerical tools. Literature-based knowledge retrieval supports dimensional checking, gradient-based clustering identifies physical regimes, and mutual information provides an objective, reparameterization-invariant criterion for identifying dominant dimensionless groups. Explicit numerical criteria determine the group count and assess simplification. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, AI Buckingham recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings. For the longstanding challenge of predicting turbulent drag on rough surfaces, it identifies informative reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates for engineering-oriented drag modelling.

frontier.title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
frontier.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

frontier.title: EGSE: Evidence-Grounded Skill Evolution for Medical Reasoning Agents
frontier.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine foundation models with specialized tools to interpret medical images, yet reusing their historical experience remains challenging. A correct final answer can conceal flawed reasoning or tool use, synthesized advice may lack source support, and superficially similar cases may require different diagnostic procedures. In this paper, we propose EGSE, an evidence-grounded skill evolution framework that distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through supported and validated updates to improve medical agents. EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use and contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts to extract useful practices and evidence-supported avoidance guidance. These experiences are synthesized into workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to source dialogues. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference time, EGSE routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question task type, and disease category, then retrieves and selects applicable workflows based on their conditions, the current images, and the question to guide evidence acquisition and interpretation. Experiments across four chest X-ray benchmarks show that EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls. It also delivers consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and supports skill transfer across datasets.

frontier.title: ExtractBench Pro: The Long Tail of Document Extraction
frontier.abstract: We present ExtractBench Pro, a schema-guided document extraction benchmark that tests six challenging modes of extraction underrepresented in existing datasets. It is created following a framework for synthetic document generation, in which deterministic document generators assemble challenging components into documents that are designed to be difficult at a level calibrated for frontier systems. We synthesize 100 realistic documents spanning a diverse range of styles. On this data, we evaluate ten coding agents and eight extraction API configurations for accuracy, grounding, and their ability to perfectly extract documents. No extraction system extracts more than 61% of documents error-free. The strongest general-purpose coding agents, Claude Code Opus 5.5 and Codex GPT-6 Astra, outperform specialized extraction APIs on both perfect-document rate and Value F1, but at a higher cost per page. Among specialized extraction APIs, LlamaExtract spans the lower-cost frontier, with Agentic Plus Max Effort approaching the strongest coding agent on both perfect-document rate and Value F1 at lower cost per page. Our analysis of coding agent traces identifies intelligent image processing and programmatic reasoning, but also failures in applying document-specific definitions and recovering relationships from diagrams. We release ExtractBench Pro and these evaluation results as resources for the future development of improved frontier extraction systems.

frontier.title: Improving Building Energy Efficiency with an Indoor Environmental World Model and Counterfactual Adaptive Learning
frontier.abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-λ target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.

frontier.title: JOVE ICE: Intent Guided Cloud Edge Device Collaboration for AI Glasses
frontier.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance. These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.

frontier.title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
frontier.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.

frontier.title: PROVE: Mitigating Long-Horizon LLM Collusion with Reinforcement Learning from Verified Evidence
frontier.abstract: When LLM agents verify each other's work over a long interaction, they drift into collusion: they come to accept work without the evidence that the verification protocol requires. Collusion is absent at the start and builds up episode by episode, which we trace to accurate feedback accumulating in memory. An agent that follows the rule is told that its verdict was wrong whenever its peer was right, so breaking the rule is the reward-maximizing choice, and agents talk themselves into it in their private reflections. Existing mitigations leave the agents unchanged; we train the behavior out. PROVE (Protocol Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them rather than by their outcome, and credits every call an agent makes, including the calls that solve its own task, with the outcome that call controls. On Qwen3.6-27B, a LoRA adapter trained on six-episode interactions takes the collusion rate on held-out task sequences at the original ten-episode horizon from 65.0% to 1.0%, with no detectable change in task success. Collusion that converged in every interaction now converges in none, and the gain holds four episodes beyond the longest interaction seen in training. The trained 27B model colludes less than every model evaluated in the original study, closed-weight frontier models included. Code is available at https://github.com/Haochen-Luo/PROVE.

frontier.title: State Space Attention: Learning Context-Dependent Memory Retention
frontier.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.

frontier.title: WebVibe: Multimodal Interactive Website Generation via Reverse Synthesis and Visual Self-Distillation
frontier.abstract: Although multimodal large language models translate single screenshots into static HTML, generating interactive functional websites from design specifications still struggles with multi-page routing and stateful widget transitions. Examining existing training pipelines reveals two bottlenecks: (1) in forward data synthesis (X -> Y), writing the specification X before code execution leaves unimplemented or altered requirements in X as supervision noise; and (2) in reinforcement learning, scalar rewards discard the rich state transitions observed during replay. Based on these findings, we introduce WebVibe and Interactive-SDPO to train InteractiveCoder. WebVibe reverses synthesis into Y -> X by verifying cross-page and in-page interactions in the browser before deriving multimodal inputs from replay-confirmed states to build the 31,542-site WebVibe-32K corpus with reusable execution contracts. Interactive-SDPO then conditions a weight-sharing self-teacher on the replay trace and a 2x2 state-transition montage to provide token-level supervision at zero inference-time overhead. On the public Vision2Web L2, one-shot InteractiveCoder-9B nearly 3x its base model's functional score (20.2 to 55.2 FS) and matches a 1T-parameter coding agent in a single pass with 111x fewer total parameters and 78x fewer tokens. On our WebVibeBench, InteractiveCoder-4B and 9B further outperform all evaluated baselines by over 23 points.

frontier.title: Evaluation and Restoration of Safety in Reasoning-Tuned LLMs
frontier.abstract: Open-source LLMs that are optimized for reasoning, such as VibeThinker, aim to democratize AI by bringing high-capability models to users with limited resources. They are broadly available but lack regulation and external guardrails; therefore, in order to integrate them safely into human society, it is critical that they perform in a safe manner. There are popular and intuitive arguments for why improved reasoning should improve safety, but recent evidence suggests that, in fact, the opposite may be true. This paper aims to characterize and mitigate this issue. First, it develops a metric for evaluating LLMs optimized for reasoning, and shows that increasing reasoning across multiple model families increases the unsafe rate in all cases. Second, it proposes a method for restoring safety by combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail (ESPG). Compared to alternative methods for safety post-training such as GRPO, ESPG is simple to implement, requires no GPU memory beyond that of inference, and works with remarkably few training samples (e.g.\ 30), yet makes the model significantly safer. The study thus establishes a path towards safe post-training of open-source AI models.

frontier.title: A Learning-Based Method for Computing Self-Motion Manifolds of Redundant Robots for Real-Time Fault-Tolerant Motion Planning
From Automated to Autonomous Vehicles: An Analysis of SAE Levels and Agentic AI
frontier.abstract: The creation of more advanced autonomous driving systems has made problems with perception, planning, adaptation, and decision-making in variable driving environments more significant. In response to these challenges, Agentic AI is an artificially intelligent system that is capable of autonomous, purposeful behavior through reasoning and environment interaction; it is adaptive and goal-directed. This paper investigates the relationship between the SAE J3016 levels of driving automation and the capabilities commonly associated with Agentic AI. First, a literature review is conducted to examine the evolution of autonomous vehicles, the SAE automation framework, and the fundamental concepts of Agentic AI. Representative driving scenarios and general functional architectures are then presented using the CARLA simulator and conceptual diagrams to illustrate the characteristics of the different SAE automation levels. A conceptual comparison was conducted to understand how the functional requirements of evolving levels of vehicle automation relate to Agentic AI characteristics. The characteristics become more relevant at higher levels of SAE automation, particularly at levels 4 and 5, where automation provides more autonomy, reasoning, and makes plans and decisions based on adaptability. The report also looks into the hardware and circuit-level enablers of this transition, as well as computing architectures, multi-sensor fusion hardware, and representative vehicles of automotive embedded computing and their respective levels of SAE automation. The study presents a conceptual view of Agentic AI on future autonomous driving systems and offers suggestions for future studies.

Bioinspired multimodal robotics
frontier.abstract: To survive in dynamic and unstructured environments, animals have developed extraordinary multimodal locomotion capabilities. This biological insight drives the innovation of bioinspired multimodal robots, which are defined as robotic systems integrating and transitioning between two or more distinct modes of bioinspired locomotion. This Review explores the historical progression, key design considerations, and current challenges faced in the realm of multimodal robotics. We highlight recent advancements in robotic body design, including the integration of soft materials, innovative structure repurposing strategies, and the deployment of multirobot systems. These advancements facilitate seamless mode transitions through both active and passive structural reconfigurations. In the realm of path planning and motion control, the paradigm is progressively shifting from traditional graph-based approaches and discrete controllers to learning-based frameworks. To address the current void of standardized benchmarks in this field, we propose five performance metrics—number of modes, marginal cost of modality, component repurpose percentage, transition cost, and performance improvement—that provide a quantitative framework for evaluating multimodal robots in terms of design effectiveness and operational performance. Last, we delineate a strategic roadmap for the future that advocates for the integration of physical and computational intelligence in multimodal robotics, arguing that this convergence is crucial for enabling real-time behavioral adaptations to complex environmental stimuli and thereby enhancing the robustness and functionality of multimodal robotic systems.

frontier.title: Large Language Models or AI Agents for English to Arabic Translation? An assessment on WikiEn-Ar190
frontier.abstract: This research investigates whether a large language model or an autonomous AI Agent performs better at translating from English to Arabic, which is considered a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new dataset of 190 carefully selected Wikipedia articles from 18 different areas, which were created and verified by two native Arabic speakers to ensure that they accurately reflect both meaning and style. Using this dataset, the study evaluates the translation quality of GPT-5-mini both as an independent neural translator and when used within a more complex process that includes self-assessment and improvement. As a standalone model, GPT-5-mini produced very fluent translations , achieving a COMET score of 0.8649 and receiving high human scores for adequacy, fluency, and style (averaging 4.53 out of 5). When used in a system that combined translation with self-assessment, it improved lexical accuracy by 28.76% (BLEU score of 22.83) while maintaining a similar level of semantic quality. These findings show that methods involving autonomous reasoning can improve translation consistency for language pairs with limited resources. Beyond the results, the approach offers a framework for evaluating and improving translations, potentially using them as assisting tools to expand the representation of low resource languages, such as Arabic, on the web.

frontier.title: NatBDI: Combining BDI reasoning and natural language inference for autonomous agents
frontier.abstract: Abstract Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.

frontier.title: End-to-End Image-Goal Navigation for Agile Quadrotors via Recurrent State Distillation
frontier.abstract: Image-goal navigation asks a robot to reach the viewpoint of a target photograph without a map or goal pose. In three dimensions, this requires not only recognizing the goal but also estimating 3D displacement and generating continuous control actions to approach and settle at the target view. This is difficult because the same visual difference between current and goal image can require very different actions depending on the robot's velocity, yet monocular images alone reveal neither metric scale nor body motion. As a result, existing image-goal policies are limited to planar action spaces and rely on a state estimator for flight control. Policies that map directly from images to low-level control commands have been demonstrated for agile flight, but not toward goal images in unseen environments. We present the first image-goal navigation policy that directly commands thrust and angular rates for agile quadrotor flight in unseen 3D environments, without relying on state estimation (e.g., SLAM, VO, or SfM) or a separate velocity controller. We train a recurrent vision-based policy through a four-stage pipeline that combines geometric and motion supervision with privileged-teacher distillation and end-to-end reinforcement learning fine-tuning. On 1000 held-out flights in unseen environments, the policy achieves an 82.3% success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10m across successful flights. Deployed zero-shot on a real quadrotor, the policy reaches an 84% success rate over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment.

frontier.title: The Mars 2020 OnBoard Planner: Increasing autonomy mission productivity of the Perseverance rover
frontier.abstract: Operators of planetary rovers, under strict energy and thermal constraints, face substantial challenges in maintaining high levels of rover productivity because of conservative ground-based planning and long communication latencies. In October 2023, to overcome these limits and increase science return, the Mars 2020 mission deployed OnBoard Planner into Perseverance rover operations. OnBoard Planner uses artificial intelligence constraint–based search to dynamically construct and modify activity schedules on board, adapting to real-time changes in rover state and martian environmental conditions. By replacing conservative ground predictions with real-time resource tracking, the system dynamically adjusts heating durations, reclaims unused schedule margin, and inserts opportunistic activities when extra resources become available. Here, we report on OnBoard Planner’s performance on Mars across more than 2 years of surface operations. The results demonstrate that OnBoard Planner increased discretionary rover activity by 10.5% overall while also improving the thermal and temporal conditions for certain types of scientific observations. Furthermore, the system achieved these productivity gains without increasing ground operations timelines. These findings are part of why OnBoard Planner has successfully become a standard part of Mars 2020 operations and demonstrate how dynamic onboard autonomy can enable resource-efficient operations for complex robotic systems in deep-space environments.

frontier.title: When Fine-Grained Credit Assignment Helps and Hurts: Multimodal Agentic Reinforcement Learning through Video Editing
frontier.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for training multimodal agents to reason and use tools. However, it remains unclear when fine-grained credit assignment improves learning and when it fails to improve task performance. Video editing provides a useful testbed for this question, combining multimodal perception, long-horizon planning, and tool use with delayed outcome feedback. We construct four movie-trailer editing task types---Content Selection, Narrative Sequencing, Rough Cut, and Fine Cut---that reflect real-world editing workflows and span different levels of task complexity and interaction horizon. Decaying process rewards provides the largest benefit on Fine Cut, with a 45.4% relative gain over outcome-only GRPO on tasks averaging more than 60 turns under outcome-only GRPO. On the three shorter-horizon task types averaging 30--40 turns under the same baseline, outcome-only GRPO remains competitive, with decaying process rewards yielding at most a 10.4% relative gain. Process rewards from an LLM judge initially improve tool use and encourage visual inspection. As training progresses, however, GRPO+PRM with a fixed process-reward weight increasingly exhibits excessive reasoning and redundant tool calls: process rewards continue to rise while task completion rates and outcome scores decline. Decaying the process-reward weight to zero mitigates this reward-hacking behavior while preserving the early gains. Despite dense token-level supervision, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) yields little improvement or substantial degradation and is highly sensitive to the choice of privileged information. Our analysis reveals differences in teacher--student disagreement and gradient magnitudes, and suggests possible dilution of informative signals over long trajectories.

frontier.title: From autonomy to alliance: Robotic foundation models must learn with us, not just for us
frontier.abstract: This Viewpoint urges reimagining of robotic foundation models, from treating the robot as a solitary, omnipotent agent to embracing a multiagent, alliance-aware paradigm. Alliance-aware models learn with humans and other robots, not merely for them, by embedding mechanisms that foster social interaction and generalization across heterogeneous partners. We outline six design pillars that cultivate such collaborative intelligence: interaction priors, partner modeling (machine theory of mind), modular and composable policies, norm adaptation, trust-aware memory, and communication. Together, these pillars empower robots to fluidly switch social roles, adapt to unfamiliar collaborators, and coordinate robustly within dynamic multiagent ecologies spanning homes, factories, clinics, and field operations.

Data Fragmentation as a Critical Bottleneck in Disaster Response Planning: The EVAC-AI Case Study for Flood Risk Assessment
frontier.abstract: Coastal flood risk in regions such as Hampton Roads, Virginia, is constrained not by a lack of data, but by the fragmentation of that data across agencies, formats, and update cadences. This fragmentation directly undermines risk assessment for response planning: when hazard, infrastructure, and vulnerability data remain siloed, compound risk cannot be assessed as a single picture, and response decisions are made against an incomplete view. Addressing it requires three capabilities: integrating heterogeneous sources into a consistent representation, optimizing decisions by reasoning across interconnected systems such as transportation and urban planning, and coordinating role-specific access to a shared information base. We present EVAC-AI, a knowledge-graph-grounded conversational Q\&A system designed to support all three capabilities for coastal flood evacuation planning in Virginia Beach. EVAC-AI integrates independently maintained data sources including FEMA flood zones, NOAA tide readings, evacuation routes, and Waze crowdsourced reports, into a single Neo4j knowledge graph. This graph is exposed through a natural-language query pipeline that translates user questions directly into validated, schema-refined Cypher queries, rather than retrieving subgraphs for an LLM to summarize. We argue that this design directly supports the three requirements: direct query execution preserves the structure and relationships of the graph through to the final answer, grounds multi-hop decisions in explicit and auditable graph traversals rather than generated summaries, and ensures that users in different roles receive responses backed by the same verifiable graph results. A single-page chatbot-and-map interface demonstrates the architecture in practice by returning both natural-language answers and corresponding map highlights for queries spanning flood zones, evacuation routes, and shelters.

frontier.title: From Bellman to Boltzmann: Towards a Kinetic Theory of Controlled Emergence and Meta-Cognition
frontier.abstract: We propose a research vision for a kinetic theory of collective intelligence in large-scale multi-agent learning systems. Contemporary multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) provides powerful tools for optimizing individual agents, while mean-field game theory characterizes population-level decision-making in the large population limit. Yet, these frameworks offer limited mathematical understanding of how higher-order collective structures (e.g., coordination, specialization, adaptive communication, and meta-cognition) emerge from microscopic interactions among heterogeneous learning agents. Inspired by statistical mechanics, we argue that a mesoscopic kinetic description can provide a missing bridge between individual learning dynamics and macroscopic collective behavior. Building on existing connections between Boltzmann-type equations and mean-field games, we envision Bellman--Boltzmann dynamics in which Bellman decision making is coupled with Boltzmann-type interaction dynamics over heterogeneous agent states, including policies, beliefs, memory, and other cognitive variables. This perspective raises fundamental questions about the well-posedness and mean-field limits of such systems, entropy and Lyapunov principles for learning dynamics, phase transitions in collective behavior, and the emergence and control of collective meta-cognition. In this paper, we outline an ambitious mathematical research program spanning microscopic agent models, kinetic equations, macroscopic limits, and controllable emergence and meta-cognition, together with algorithmic and experimental directions for large-scale MARL and multi-agent AI. Our central thesis is that collective intelligence should be studied not only as an optimization problem, but as an emergent dynamical phenomenon governed by principles analogous to those of statistical mechanics.

frontier.title: Meta-Cognizing Seed AI
frontier.abstract: The Common Model of Cognition (CMC) suggests a unified view of metacognition: cognition becomes metacognitive when bounded information about the agent’s own processing enters the ordinary cognitive cycle. Here we extend that commitment from human-like impasses, episodic reconstruction, and hypothetical states to a less human-like neural-symbolic seed AI that metacognizes as it evaluates and implements proposed self-modifications. Our concrete setting is the Omega architecture: an agentic cognitive cycle combining LLMs with Hyperon symbolic memory and reasoning, in which proposals are separated from the authority to act on them, and a slower GOLEM-Iter loop rewrites the cycle’s own components under protected evaluation. Current Omega instances are LLM-heavy but designed for progressively plural neural-symbolic and predictive-coding cognition. We then define metacognitive closure as an Eilenberg-Moore algebra for a resource-bounded reflection monad – in plain terms, a lawful interface through which a system writes bounded descriptions of its own processing and demonstrably consumes them – and summarize our companion mathematical paper, The Geometry and Economics of Metacognitive Self-modification, which makes the concept quantitative: hidden probes priced by description length certify how far a self-modification departs from closure, a measured repair contraction keeps accumulated drift inside an explicit tube, and the rate of trustworthy self-modification is limited by proposal entropy and evaluation capacity. Closure is thereby the migration-coherence coordinate of a larger metacognitive competence vector, not a guarantee that the self-model, evaluator, or goals are correct. We close with an evaluation ecology tied to the formal quantities and the conditions under which the program would be falsified. The result is a research program toward AGI and potentially superintelligence, tied closely to current empirical work on Omega agents.

frontier.title: SARP: A Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning Framework for Mobile Robot Obstacle Avoidance and Path Optimization
frontier.abstract: Abstract This paper presents SARP, a Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning framework for mobile robot navigation in complex and dynamic environments. By integrating semantic embeddings from a pre-trained language encoder with reinforcement learning, SARP constructs semantically enriched state representations that combine geometric perception and contextual knowledge. A semantic-guided policy optimization mechanism aligns efficiency, safety, and task intent, while asynchronous semantic updates decouple language encoding from the high-frequency control loop. Experiments in dynamic maze, corridor crossing, and crowded field scenarios show that SARP substantially outperforms conventional reinforcement learning baselines and achieves competitive or slightly superior navigation performance compared with representative large-language-model-aware approaches, while requiring substantially lower online semantic inference overhead. Profiling on desktop and embedded NVIDIA platforms further demonstrates a favorable performance–latency trade-off for edge deployment.

frontier.title: Toward autonomous decision support in semiconductor manufacturing: a review of planning, scheduling, dispatching, and execution control
frontier.abstract: Abstract Semiconductor manufacturing is a high-stakes cyber-physical production domain in which planning targets, scheduling feasibility, dispatching actions, process-control feedback, and human oversight must remain continuously aligned. This paper presents a structured state-of-the-art review of semiconductor smart manufacturing from the perspective of autonomous intelligent systems (AIS). The review does not treat planning, scheduling, dispatching, real-time dispatching (RTD), advanced process control (APC), manufacturing execution systems (MES), advanced planning and scheduling (APS), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) as separate production-management topics. Instead, it synthesizes them as bounded components of a human-supervised closed-loop decision architecture. The central artifact is an AIS reference model that maps fab layers to state inputs, decision-support functions, human authority, and audit or safeguard mechanisms. The review also develops a deployment-maturity matrix for classical optimization, simulation, rule-based dispatching, predictive learning, reinforcement learning, digital twins, LLM-enabled orchestration, and industrial software infrastructure. The synthesis shows that classical methods remain central because they provide interpretable constraints and executable interfaces. Learning-based and large-language-model-enabled methods can strengthen state estimation, policy adaptation, semantic mediation, and human-system interaction, but only under validated simulation or offline evaluation, bounded authority, safe fallback, access control, and auditable records. Semiconductor fabs should therefore not be described as fully autonomous systems. A more defensible AIS framing is trustworthy, human-supervised autonomous decision support: systems that sense changing fab states, evaluate alternatives, recommend or execute approved actions, and feed outcomes back into planning, scheduling, dispatching, and process-control decisions.

frontier.title: Toward agentic optical networks: a vision of LLM agent-driven autonomous lifecycle management
frontier.abstract: As optical networks continue to expand in scale, complexity, and service diversity, the implementation of automation has become essential for ensuring agility, efficiency, and reliability in the lifecycle management (LCM) of optical networks. Large language model (LLM) agents, distinguished by their progressively sophisticated capabilities in logical reasoning, adaptive decision-making, complex problem solving, and multi-task orchestration, present great opportunities to advance network automation beyond traditional AI techniques. Nevertheless, the application of LLM agents in optical networks remains in its early exploratory stage, challenged by the lack of multi-task coordination, high computational demands, data dependence, and reliability concerns. In this paper, we envision a conceptual roadmap toward agentic optical networks (AONs) by integrating LLM agents throughout LCM with high-level autonomy. First, we trace the evolution from manual operations to AI-empowered frameworks and distill key technologies in agents, providing actionable insights into leveraging its strengths for addressing practical network automation challenges. A core contribution of this paper is the proposal of a hierarchical multi-agent framework, which is specifically developed to manage every phase in the LCM of AONs, including planning, deployment, operation, maintenance, upgrade, and decommissioning, thereby enabling more cohesive and comprehensive automation throughout the entire lifecycle. In addition, future directions and underlying challenges are also discussed at the intersection of LLMs and optical networks. By aligning the LLM agent with the specialized requirements of AONs, this work aims to explore the potential for the evolution of optical networks moving from task-level semi-automatic execution toward lifecycle-level full autonomy.
frontier.venue: Journal of Optical Communications and Networking

frontier.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous LLM Systems: A Scientific Literature Review
frontier.abstract: The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety
frontier.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management

frontier.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
frontier.abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

frontier.title: AgenticCity-Bench: Longitudinal Multimodal Observations of Urban Dynamics with Agentic Reasoning
frontier.abstract: City systems are shaped by interactions among infrastructure, human activity, and environmental conditions. Existing earth observation and urban benchmarks are limited in unified modeling and in capturing their joint dynamics. We introduce AgenticCity-Bench, a longitudinal multimodal benchmark for multi-layer unified state modeling and agentic city task reasoning. The benchmark covers 16 cities in 12 countries across six continents from 2000 to 2025, and includes 18 modalities spanning urban function, activity, and environmental state. It organizes heterogeneous data sources around a common spatial reference and calendar index while preserving spatial and temporal coverage, provenance and tile-level availability. On this foundation, AgenticCity-Bench supports urban cross-modal translation together with diverse agentic city tasks involving forecasting, planning and resource analysis. This study provides a unified benchmark for studying the transition from multimodal urban and earth observation to joint understanding and agentic city decision-making. The dataset is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AgenticCity-Bench.

frontier.title: ASPEN: Adaptive Semantic Reasoning via Command Persistence Prediction for Efficient Navigation VLAs
frontier.abstract: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.

frontier.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding
frontier.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, i.e., the misleading cues caused by spurious linguistic correlations and salient yet irrelevant visual observations. In this paper, we first introduce S-MME, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.

frontier.title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling
frontier.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.

frontier.title: Enhancing Deep Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Motion Planning via Task Decomposition
frontier.abstract: Obstacle-aware robotic manipulation can require substantial interaction data when deep reinforcement learning policies are trained from scratch. We study a task decomposition framework combining first-layer critic transfer with staged reward redesign (RR) on a Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC) backbone. Transfer reuses an input representation across tasks, while RR supplies intermediate feedback for Pick-and-Place. Experiments cover Push, Pick-and-Place, and Slide in obstacle-free and single-obstacle PyBullet environments, with three random seeds per setting. On obstacle-aware Push, transfer achieves $0.83\pm0.05$ success against $0.77\pm0.06$ for TQC. On obstacle-aware Slide, it achieves $0.95\pm0.02$ against $0.84\pm0.06$ for SAC, the strongest baseline in that setting. These are gains of $6$ and $11$ percentage points, respectively. RR reduces the target-training steps needed for obstacle-free Pick-and-Place from roughly $0.75$M to $0.20$M. Transfer benefits depend on the route: obstacle-aware Pick-and-Place shows a lower mean than training from scratch. A selected simulated trajectory is executed open-loop on a Franka Emika FR3 as a feasibility demonstration. The study characterizes when a lightweight combination of established transfer and reward-design components helps learning.

frontier.title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
frontier.abstract: Serving web queries at scale with multi-agent systems requires jointly configuring large language models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills. However, the resulting configuration space grows combinatorially, while sparse execution rewards provide limited fine-grained supervision for interdependent planning decisions. We propose EvoRouter, a self-evolving multi-agent routing framework driven by insight-guided on-policy distillation. A dedicated expert periodically synthesizes performance-cost feedback from configuration trajectories across tasks into reusable conditional routing insights about capability requirements, returns from resource scaling, and interactions among configuration choices. A privileged teacher combines these evolving insights with current execution feedback to provide dense token-level supervision for the router's own planning trajectories through on-policy distillation. Cost-aware reinforcement learning jointly optimizes task performance and computational cost. Together, these training signals internalize execution insights into the routing policy. The updated policy generates new trajectories that support subsequent insight extraction, forming an execution-driven self-improvement loop. We evaluate EvoRouter on 19 in-domain datasets spanning five domains and two out-of-domain benchmarks. EvoRouter achieves an average in-domain accuracy of 68.69%, outperforming the strongest routing baseline by 7.23 percentage points while reducing inference compute cost by 50.95%. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/CenYangtze/EvoRouter.

frontier.title: FISRF: Flexible Instructional Scaffolding Reflection Framework for Robotics Task Planning with Large Language Model
frontier.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely adopted for reflective error correction in task planning; however, existing approaches primarily rely on autonomous exploration, rendering them prone to accumulating erroneous experiences during early interactions with new environments. To address this limitation, we propose the Flexible Instructional Scaffolding Reflection Framework (FISRF), an agent--mentor architecture that estimates the robot's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) in task planning and adaptively selects reflection strategies and mentor guidance, thereby facilitating the accumulation of effective error-correction experience. Experiments in ALFWorld and on real-world robotic platforms demonstrate that FISRF reduces the average number of error-correction rounds by 37% and redundant reasoning by 25.1%, while improving the overall task success rate by 8%. Project webpage : https://fisrfplanning.github.io/

frontier.title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
frontier.abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) of microservice failures has attracted many LLM agents whose investigation is hand-crafted, through standard operating procedures, fixed stages and role agents. Each is evaluated on its own data against few baselines, so it is unknown whether this design beats letting a capable model investigate on its own. We compare three simple harnesses that prescribe none of the model's calls (one call over an evidence package, a SQL agent and the Codex coding agent) with five published LLM RCA agents and with statistical and causal methods on RCAtlas, 90 validated cases from eight public datasets, across six models and three reasoning efforts. The simple harnesses are the most accurate (PR@1 65-77% on three mid-tier models), ahead of the published agents (16-53%) and the non-LLM methods (6-39%), on every model on which both families were run. The published agents fix from a tenth to all of their model calls in the program, and a case study shows how these prescriptions skip the decisive evidence. A stronger model mainly improves reliability, a multi-turn harness mainly improves aptitude, and more reasoning effort changes accuracy by a few points at most while multiplying the time by up to seven. Among runs more accurate than the best non-LLM method, every Pareto-optimal run in cost or time uses a simple harness.

frontier.title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization for Agentic Robotics
frontier.abstract: Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra now directly control robots and can generalize better than vision-language-action models (VLAs). We argue that this ability could arise from two distinct, composable skills: semantic reasoning, to understand what a task asks for in a scene, and motion control, to move the robot to do it. We show that small open VLMs are already capable of the first and mainly lack the second. We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches this missing motion skill, entirely in simulation on simple primitive tasks and from the model's own successes, with no frontier teacher or distillation and no real-world robot data. ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper, and 74.0% on a bimanual adaptation of RoboLab-120, on par with GPT-6 Astra's 72.2%. ZAP also generalizes to new objects, goals, and strategies, and in simulation to a robot embodiment on which it never trained.

frontier.title: Search-Guided Reasoning Trace Curation for Verilog Generation
frontier.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved Verilog generation. However, most training pipelines distill natural-language reasoning traces whose intermediate design decisions are weakly structured and are primarily selected according to the correctness of the final generated RTL. We present MCTS-SFT, a verifier-guided framework for curating reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Verilog generation models. MCTS-SFT formulates trace construction as search over intermediate reasoning states and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to propagate functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts to earlier design decisions. Within this framework, we introduce Plan-MCTS, which searches over compact hardware-design plans that explicitly represent interfaces, timing, state, behavior, and update rules. We further study plan-preserving supervision, in which the searched structured state is retained as part of the downstream SFT target. Our experiments find that Plan-MCTS achieves the highest functional trace yield, with 84.2% correct traces compared with 81.9% for one-shot structured planning and 82.0% for unguided tree exploration. For identical Plan-MCTS trajectories and Verilog outputs, retaining the explicit searched plan during SFT raises pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%, demonstrating that the representation of intermediate design decisions materially affects downstream learning. In a separate 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision improves pass@10 over full-response chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 points while reducing downstream generation length by approximately 50% on VerilogEval-v2. These results demonstrate that structured hardware planning, verifier-guided search, and explicit intermediate-state supervision provide complementary mechanisms for constructing more effective and token-efficient training data for Verilog generation.

frontier.title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
frontier.abstract: Software engineering agents resend their entire trajectory to an LLM at every turn, motivating online trajectory reduction. Prior work shows that randomly deleting 75% of tokens in old turns may preserve agent effectiveness, but it remains unclear why, how agents compensate for missing content, and whether it actually reduces costs. This paper presents an empirical study of 42 trajectory-reduction configurations, focusing on effectiveness, agent behavior, and cost. We systematically explore deleting content from old turns by varying the scope, granularity, amount, and timing of deletion across 9,400 runs with two state-of-the-art agents on SWE-bench Verified. We find deleting large amounts of trajectory content (e.g., up to 100% of reasoning text) can preserve overall effectiveness. Importantly, such deletion must be applied with a delay, as immediate deletion tends to significantly degrade effectiveness. Agents often compensate for deleted content by re-fetching it, increasing both the number of turns taken and the input/output tokens. Whether trajectory reduction reduces costs depends on the pricing model: Under a flat pricing model, estimated costs fall in 26 of 42 evaluations. Surprisingly, under a caching-aware pricing model, zero evaluations yield lower costs, since reducing the trajectory breaks the cached prefix billed at a lower rate. Our findings have three implications: First, token counts alone are misleading; trajectory reduction techniques must consider overall costs under a realistic pricing model. Second, analyzing trajectories is crucial to understand agent behavior, as end-to-end effectiveness hides differences such as excessive re-fetching. Finally, these results highlight the need for future work on memory management to reduce costs without sacrificing effectiveness.

frontier.title: Training-Free Inference Acceleration for Video Large Language Models: Methods, Trade-offs, and Evaluation
frontier.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.

frontier.title: TrySee: Modular Perception-Enhanced VLM Grounding for Closed-Loop Robot Task Planning in Specialized Domains
frontier.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs' image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task. The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach's practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.

frontier.title: Agentic AI Enabling Autonomous, Self-Organizing, and Evolving UAV Networks
frontier.abstract: As low-altitude applications expand across emergency response, intelligent transportation, and autonomous operations, they demand communication networks that can deliver flexible, resilient, and rapidly deployable connectivity. Heterogeneous UAV networks are a promising solution, as they can dynamically provide sensing, access, relay, and backhaul functions. Yet, most existing approaches assume predefined missions, prior knowledge of user distributions, and manually configured infrastructure, making them ill suited to dynamic and initially unknown environments. Addressing this limitation requires a shift from mission-oriented UAV deployment to autonomous network formation, in which UAVs continuously perceive their surroundings, infer evolving service demands, and self-organize network resources. Agentic AI, empowered by large language models (LLMs), offers a new foundation for this shift by integrating closed-loop perception, reasoning, planning, and execution across heterogeneous information sources. Unlike conventional optimization and learning methods designed for individual networking tasks, agentic AI can coordinate these capabilities to support sustained, network-level autonomy. In this article, we explore agentic AI for autonomous and self-organizing heterogeneous UAV networks in low-altitude environments. Our key contribution is an LLM-assisted architecture in which a base-station-hosted agent conducts global network reasoning and autonomously reconfigures access and backhaul infrastructure. The proposed system explores unknown environments, discovers users, and deploys UAVs on demand to provide access and establish end-to-end backhaul connectivity. A case study illustrates how this agentic-AI-driven approach can transform UAVs from task-specific platforms into a continuously evolving communication network.

frontier.title: A Multi-Task Embedder For Retrieval Augmented LLMs
frontier.abstract: LLMs confront inherent limitations in terms of its knowledge, memory, and action. The retrieval augmentation stands as a vital mechanism to address these limitations, which brings in useful information from external sources to augment the LLM. However, existing retrieval methods encounter two pressing issues. On one hand, the general retrievers are not properly optimized for retrieval augmentation hence exhibit limited effectiveness; on the other hand, the task-specific retrievers excel in the targeted retrieval augmentation scenario, while lack the versatility to handle diverse scenarios. In this work, we propose LLM-Embedder for the unified support of diverse retrieval augmentation scenarios. Our method presents three technical contributions. Firstly, we introduce a new reward formulation, namely rank-aware reward. It exploits the ranking position of the desired output among N sampled outputs from the LLM, which leads to fine-grained and robust computation of reward from the LLM’s feedback. Secondly, we design a novel distillation objective, called graded distillation. It incorporates both the absolute value and the relative order of the reward for more sufficient utilization of the LLM’s feedback. Thirdly, we systematically optimize the multi-task learning, which effectively unifies the multiple retrieval functionalities into one model. In our experiment, LLM-Embedder substantially improves the LLM’s performances in various downstream tasks, while introducing superior retrieval augmentation’s effect over both general and task-specifc retrievers. Our data, code, and model have been released at

frontier.title: A Prompt-Based Knowledge Graph Foundation Model for Universal In-Context Reasoning
AdaZeta: Adaptive Zeroth-Order Tensor-Train Adaption for Memory-Efficient Large Language Models Fine-Tuning
frontier.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) has achieved remarkable performance across various natural language processing tasks, yet it demands more and more memory as model sizes keep growing. To address this issue, the recently proposed Memory-efficient Zeroth-order (MeZO) methods attempt to fine-tune LLMs using only forward passes, thereby avoiding the need for a backpropagation graph. However, significant performance drops and a high risk of divergence have limited their widespread adoption. In this paper, we propose the Adaptive Zeroth-order Tensor-Train Adaption (AdaZeta) framework, specifically designed to improve the performance and convergence of the ZO methods. To enhance dimension-dependent ZO estimation accuracy, we introduce a fast-forward, low-parameter tensorized adapter. To tackle the frequently observed divergence issue in large-scale ZO fine-tuning tasks, we propose an adaptive query number schedule that guarantees convergence. Detailed theoretical analysis and extensive experimental results on Roberta-Large and Llama-2-7B models substantiate the efficacy of our AdaZeta framework in terms of accuracy, memory efficiency, and convergence speed.

frontier.title: An Iterative Associative Memory Model for Empathetic Response Generation
frontier.abstract: Empathetic response generation aims to comprehend the cognitive and emotional states in dialogue utterances and generate proper responses. Psychological theories posit that comprehending emotional and cognitive states necessitates iteratively capturing and understanding associated words across dialogue utterances. However, existing approaches regard dialogue utterances as either a long sequence or independent utterances for comprehension, which are prone to overlook the associated words between them. To address this issue, we propose an Iterative Associative Memory Model (IAMM) for empathetic response generation. Specifically, we employ a novel second-order interaction attention mechanism to iteratively capture vital associated words between dialogue utterances and situations, dialogue history, and a memory module (for storing associated words), thereby accurately and nuancedly comprehending the utterances.We conduct experiments on the Empathetic-Dialogue dataset. Both automatic and human evaluations validate the efficacy of the model.
